docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: In this project, we discussed discrimination, economy and work culture in Indian society. We put a light on structural inequality in India, how India was created, subsequently partitioned and why these events shape today's power dynamics, how leaders like Ambedkar and Nehru built the foundation of modern India, how does caste, class, religion and gender influence people's lives and what barriers they face to achieve success, how people are trapped in a privatized and exclusion driven Indian economy, and problems in formal and informal sector in India.

docs.title: Who is NATIONALIST? (PART 1/3)
docs.text:
Imagine a future where Earth is one government, and a child in 2150 calls you "anti-Earth" because you loved your country. That wouldn't be fair. You cannot betray what does not yet exist.

The same applies to calling medieval rulers "anti-national." But let's play along and judge them by today's standards. By that logic, Khilji and Aurangzeb were the greatest NATIONALISTS.

They safeguarded India from foreign rule and made India so rich its GDP surpassed China's. Now you have a choice - call them nationalists and contradict every textbook, or call them anti-national and watch your standard collapse.

Let me open your eyes to your own HYPOCRISY

Can a nationalist cheer for DESTROYING PAKISTAN but ignore local INJUSTICE?

Yes.

Nationalism points outward - find an enemy, blame outsiders.

This is easy and exciting. But fixing internal injustice - caste apartheid, hunger, 1% holding 40% of wealth is hard. It requires looking at ourselves. Nationalism rewards those who look away. The same person who rages about borders is silent about the Dalit child denied water.

IMPORTANT COMMENTARY:-

Nationalism can fight empire and give dignity to the colonized, but it has never built a just society. It creates winners and losers, insiders and outsiders, hierarchy with a flag on top. If nationalism cannot deliver equality and demands loyalty above humanity, why give it your deepest faith?
  • Habeeb - nationalism is a concept that enables unity against oppression based on human values, culture, geography... To assume nationalism is undying blind loyalty to a flag or authority is the perversion of nationalism.
  • Yash - the main conversation should be "what is the utility of nationalism"
  • Habeeb - the question is "Why Nationalism" why not "Patriotism" - there's a big difference between both, yet most people conflate both.

One is saying "I'm owned by my father and another is saying I'm owned by my tribe" .. both are true .. humans can't EXIST as individual, humans are mammals so they live in the group. The Question is : ARE humans BEYOND MAMMALS if YES then HOW and HOW much ??

  • Akhilesh - It seems you need social context. Though the attempt is good, the thought process seems to be deficient. How? Your post rightly points to caste injustice, hunger, and inequality as urgent realities that demand attention. These are issues no society can afford to ignore. But the framing of nationalism here feels alienated from lived social struggles. Nationalism in India was not merely about “pointing outward”—it was also the force that mobilized millions for independence, built solidarity across regions, and anchored welfare reforms. To dismiss it wholesale is to erase the social context in which it operated as a vehicle for justice. The speculative “Earth Government 2150” analogy and the retrofitting of nationalism onto medieval rulers reveal a thought process that is abstract, irresponsible, and impractical. It retreats into rhetorical provocation rather than engaging with the messy realities of how communities actually negotiate identity and reform. The real challenge is not to pit nationalism against equality, but to reimagine nationalism in inclusive, socially grounded terms—one that erases internal hierarchies while still mobilizing collective strength.

What would help here is to go deeper into how ideologies are birthed - why do we have a distinct Pakistan and distinct India? Nonetheless, even in a utopia, you'd still have small geographical units with a local government (think Panchayats) because presiding over a large landmass is just inefficient. docs.title: Savarkar’s Exclusionary Logic (Part 2/3)
docs.text:
Savarkar said a true nation needs two things -

Pitrabhumi (fatherland) and Punyabhumi (holy land).

Fatherland means ancestral land. Holy land means religious land. According to him, only those who have both can be real citizens. Everyone else is less than full citizen.

First, Muslims and Christians. They may have fatherland - they were born here, their ancestors lived here. But they do not have Punyabhumi because their holy land is Mecca or Jerusalem.

So according to this idea, they will always be outsiders. Even if their family lived in India for a thousand years.

Second, lower castes. Many of them never owned land. No fatherland. No ancestral property. So they are also less than full citizens.

Now ask yourself - does putting nationalism on top solve inequality?

No. It does nothing.

A Dalit child still has no land. A Muslim family still has no holy land here. Their daily problems - hunger, no water, no job, caste violence - remain exactly the same.

But nationalism gives you a distraction.

It says - forget your empty stomach. Forget your daughter cannot go to school. Look outside. There is an enemy. There is a foreign threat. Be united against them.

IMPORTANT COMMENTARY:-

  • Sajal - This actually worsens the problems. When you put nationalism on top, all energy goes into finding outsiders to blame. No energy goes into fixing what is broken inside.
  • Tejaswini - Inequality is faced even by those who fulfill both of Savarkar’s criteria. The so-called ‘outsiders’ can survive and live comfortably in a nation, while a citizen of that same nation may still face inequality.
  • Sajal - In what sense? Please elaborate.
  • Tejaswini - Inequality is not determined by whether someone fulfills Savarkar’s criteria or not. Even those who have both Pitrabhumi and Punyabhumi (for example, many Hindus) still face poverty, caste discrimination, lack of education, and unemployment. So fulfilling both conditions does not guarantee equality or dignity. At the same time, people who are labelled as “outsiders” under this idea can still live stable and comfortable lives in the same country. So the real issue is........inequality depends more on socio-economic factors like class, caste, access to resources and opportunities, not on religious or civilizational identity. We often assume that those who fit the criteria are also able to survive better, but in the current scenario, survival is determined by socio-economic factors, not by who belongs to the nation and who does not. Savarkar’s idea does not fit well in today’s context.
  • Sajal - Obviously because Savarkar's idea of nationalism was never implemented. Hindu mahasabha never got to rule. Today's right wing power operates within the constitutional framework and lack the authority to bring radical changes. The point here is to challenge this very idea which is being propagated through other means.

docs.title: Tata, Birla & Jains - Anti Nationals? (Part 3/3)
docs.text:
During British rule, figures like Tata, Birla, and Jains cooperated with the British. They ran businesses. They made profits. They benefited from a system that drained India's wealth and kept Indians under foreign rule.

By today's nationalist standards, what would you call them? Collaborators? Exploiters? Anti-national?

But here is the twist. After independence, the same families became nation-builders. They built industries. They created jobs. They donated to education and science. Today, we call them visionaries.

The lower castes - almost 80% of the population - never owned much of that wealth. The land, the gold, the trade, the resources - all were controlled by upper castes and elites. So when the British looted India, they were mostly looting from the already rich. The poor remained poor before, during, and after the British.

So what changed after independence? The same rich families remained rich. They just switched from British masters to Indian masters. Their wealth stayed intact. Their position stayed intact.

Now watch how nationalism works.

If you criticize Tata and Birla, nationalists will call you anti-national. They will say - these are our icons. They built modern India. Do not speak against them.

But if you point out that they cooperated with the British, nationalists will say - that was business. Everyone did it. Do not judge the past by today's standards.

So the same people get protection from both sides. Nationalism never asks - did their wealth come from exploitation? Did the system they benefited from keep the poor, poor?

Nationalism only asks - are they ours? Then we defend them.

Nehru Report
docs.text:
Before 1916, Hindus and Muslims didn't even have a shared political agreement on how to live together in one country.

What happened in 1916?

Jinnah (yes, that Jinnah) brought both sides together. Lucknow Pact happened. That was the first time Hindus and Muslims formally sat down and said, "Okay, let's figure this out."

Before that? Separate tracks. Separate electorates. No shared vision.

The real game-changer - 1928

Now here's the part no one talks about.

NEHRU REPORT

For the first time ever, Indians sat down and wrote - Freedom of speech, Freedom of religion, Equality before law, One person, one vote (mostly), No discrimination by caste, religion, or gender

This was the first time "India" meant something inclusive.

Not 1947. Not 1950.

1928.

The India we actually live in – the secular, constitutional one – came from Gandhi, Nehru, and that 1928 report.

docs.title: Partition (1947)
docs.text:
In 1937, Congress swept the elections. Huge victory.

By 1946, most Muslims voted for Pakistan.

What went wrong?

Two things. The Poona Pact (1932) and then Congress's own rule (1937-39).

Let me explain.

First, the Poona Pact (1932)

British said "separate electorates for Dalits and Muslims." Ambedkar wanted it. Gandhi said no.

Ambedkar had to give in. Signed the Poona Pact. Joint electorates with reservations instead of separate ones.

Was it necessary? Maybe. Separate electorates led to Pakistan later. So Gandhi wasn't completely wrong.

But here's the cost - Caste inequality became INVISIBLE. We pretended joint electorates fixed everything. It didn't. We're still paying for that today.

docs.text:
We know Ambedkar for reservations. We should know him for the RBI.

Most discussions around Dr. B.R. Ambedkar begin and end with social justice and the Constitution. But his sharpest work was in economics - specifically, monetary policy.

In 1923, Ambedkar wrote The Problem of the Rupee while at the London School of Economics. His argument was simple but radical for its time:

👉 India must control its own currency.

👉 Monetary decisions should not be made in London.

👉 India needed its own central bank.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was formed in 1935. The British never gave him credit. But historical evidence suggests the Hilton Young Commission (1926) was shaped by his work.

Yet today, when we hear "Ambedkar," most minds go to reservation debates - often reduced to jokes or resentment.

The real loss is ours.

We have ignored one of India's finest economic minds. And as a result, we still debate currency sovereignty, still depend on the USD like we once depended on the British Pound, and still haven't built economic systems rooted in our own demography and national interest.

Ambedkar wasn't just a social reformer. He was a political economist who understood that without monetary freedom, there is no real freedom.

Everyone loves to attack Nehru today. Right-wing calls him a socialist fool. Left-wing says he sold out to capitalism.

Both are wrong.

Here's what Nehru actually believed - and why it makes everyone uncomfortable:

He rejected pure capitalism → because it creates crony monopolies and deepens caste-based inequality.

He rejected pure communism → because it kills efficiency, innovation, and turns humans into machines.

He chose Fabian Socialism - nationalise key industries, prioritise rationality over politics, build public healthcare and education.

Now here's the important part:

Nehru supported reservations. But he also warned against them.

He said reservations are necessary to give backward communities a fair start. But if they become a permanent crutch on caste lines, the "creamy layer" will capture everything - and society will never get rid of caste.

His solution?

👉 Education.

👉 Economic opportunity.

👉 Decentralisation.

👉 Not just job quotas forever.

He also said something that would get him cancelled today:

"Caste groupings are even more dangerous than political groupings. Democracy cannot thrive in a society marked by casteism and communalism."

So let me ask you:

If Nehru was so wrong, why is every single problem he predicted - crony capitalism, creamy layer capture, regional inequality, caste violence - now worse than ever?

Just 5–6% of India’s population controls nearly one-third of the nation’s wealth.

Let me explain what the numbers actually say.

India has about 140 crore people.

Of these, only 12–15% live in Tier 1 cities (places like Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Kolkata, Ahmedabad, etc.).

But that small group controls roughly 45% of the nation's total wealth.

Now look inside Tier 1 cities:

The top 5 cities (Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad) have a population similar to the next 15 Tier 1 cities combined - roughly 7–9 crore vs 9–11 crore.

Yet the top 5 contribute nearly double the GDP (17–19% of national GDP vs 8–10%) and hold 65–70% of all Tier 1 wealth.

Zoom out to the national level:

The top 5 cities alone - just 5–6% of India's population - control nearly one-third of the country's wealth.

What about the rest?

The remaining 85–88% of Indians - living in Tier 2, Tier 3, and rural areas - share the other half of the wealth. Their average annual income is about ₹2.2–3.2 lakh, roughly half of what someone in a top metro earns (₹4.5–6.5 lakh).

Conclusion -

We are not spreading wealth across India. We are stacking it in a handful of postal codes.

India's economy is NOT meritocratic

Here's why.

IT / Startups / Finance → Upper-caste Hindus (Brahmins, Baniyas & Kayasths)

Why? Colonial legacy gave them English education first. That turned into urban jobs through social mobility.

Trade / small business → Baniyas, Jains and Marwaris

Why? Generational capital + community credit networks. If your family hasn't been trading for generations, you don't get the loan. Period.

Government jobs → Upper caste + reserved categories

Why? Reservation helps SC/ST/OBC enter. But total jobs are tiny (\~35k annually). Upper castes still dominate the top posts.

Gig economy (Zomato, Uber, Swiggy) → OBCs, SC/ST, Muslims

Why? Low barrier to entry - no degree, no network, no capital. But here's the catch: no security, no growth, no retirement. It's inclusion without dignity.

Informal labor (domestic work, construction, driving) → SC/ST, OBCs, Muslims, especially women

Why? Because formal jobs actively discriminate. When no one else hires you, you take what's left.

Conclusion - Upper castes captured the knowledge economy through early English education (a colonial gift).

Then they used social networks to keep it.

Everyone else got either reservation (too few seats) or informal/gig work (too little security).

docs.title: Business Hurdles
docs.text:
You cannot start a business in India.

Here's why

India's MSME numbers look like a success story.

📊 7.83 crore registered enterprises

📊 31.1% of GDP

📊 49% of exports

📊 32.8 crore jobs

But let's ask an uncomfortable question:

Who gets access to the credit that makes these businesses possible?

Because banks lend to those with:

· Land titles (which Dalit, Adivasi, and OBC families historically were denied)

· Existing CIBIL scores (which require prior access to formal finance)

· Collateral (urban property, not rural homesteads)

· Male guarantors (women are routinely asked to bring a husband or father)

The result is a massive ₹30 lakh crore credit gap.

And it falls disproportionately on:

➡️ Rural entrepreneurs – No bank branch nearby. Land is often oral or disputed.

➡️ Lower-caste individuals – Systemic denial of asset ownership means no collateral to offer.

➡️ Women – Required to produce male co-signers even for small MUDRA loans.

➡️ First-generation learners & workers – No family property, no financial literacy pipeline.

So when we say "MSMEs are the backbone of India's economy" – we must ask:

Whose backbone?

Because right now, the system is designed to work for the urban upper-caste male who already has family land, a bank relationship, and someone to co-sign.

The Dalit woman making pickles in a village?

The OBC welder renting a shed?

The Adivasi farmer trying to start a small agro-processing unit?

They don't lack skill or effort.

They lack privilege disguised as creditworthiness.

Real inclusion means:

✅ Moving away from collateral-based lending

✅ Aggressive rural branch expansion

✅ Gender-blind guarantee schemes (no male co-signer)

✅ Caste-disaggregated data on loan rejections

Until then, our MSME growth story will remain impressive but deeply unequal.

Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Ahmedabad.

The urban middle class in these cities carries the nation's tax burden - while large parts of the country contribute almost nothing.

The same 1.5–1.8 crore salaried Indians -

· Pay tax at source

· Can't claim cash expenses

· Can't "show less income"

· Get stuck in the 30% slab while saving little

The government calls this a "widening tax base."

In reality, they've just tightened the net around the only people who can't escape.
